# Evaluation pitfalls

A number in a paper is only comparable to another number if both survived the
checks below. Each entry names the work that established it and gives a test you
can run in an afternoon.

## `block-design` — Block design leakage in EEG visual classification

**Applies to:** EEG

**What happens.** In the Spampinato et al. (2017) EEG-ImageNet paradigm, all images of a class were presented in one contiguous block. Slow non-stimulus drift within a block is enough to identify the class, so a classifier can reach very high accuracy without using any visual information at all.

**Why it breaks comparison.** Accuracies reported on that dataset (and on any derivative that keeps the block structure) do not measure visual decoding and must not be compared against trial-randomised datasets such as THINGS-EEG2.

**Established by:** `li2021perils`

**How to check.** Shuffle the class labels within a block. If accuracy stays high, you are decoding drift.

---

## `teacher-forcing` — Teacher forcing left on at evaluation in EEG-to-text

**Applies to:** EEG/MEG

**What happens.** A large fraction of published EEG-to-text results feed the ground-truth previous token into the decoder at test time. The model is scored on next-token prediction given the true prefix, not on generating the sentence.

**Why it breaks comparison.** Reported BLEU/ROUGE are close to what the same model produces from pure noise input. Numbers obtained this way are not comparable with free-running generation and should be labelled as such in any table.

**Established by:** `jo2024areeegtext`

**How to check.** Replace the brain input with Gaussian noise. If the metrics barely move, teacher forcing is doing the work.

---

## `repeat-averaging` — Averaging stimulus repeats at test time

**Applies to:** fMRI

**What happens.** NSD test images were each viewed three times. Some papers average the three trials before decoding, some decode from a single trial.

**Why it breaks comparison.** Averaging raises SNR substantially. A 3-repeat number and a single-trial number are different tasks.

**How to check.** Look for "averaged over repetitions" in the evaluation subsection, not the dataset subsection.

---

## `retrieval-pool` — Retrieval pool size not held constant

**Applies to:** fMRI/EEG/MEG

**What happens.** Top-1 image retrieval accuracy depends directly on how many distractors are in the pool (300-way, 982-way and full-test-set retrieval all appear in the literature).

**Why it breaks comparison.** Retrieval numbers are meaningless without the pool size next to them.

**How to check.** Every retrieval cell in a comparison table needs an explicit N.

---

## `subject-specific-vs-cross` — Subject-specific models compared against cross-subject models

**Applies to:** fMRI/EEG/MEG

**What happens.** Most strong reconstruction results train one model per subject on tens of hours of that subject's data. Cross-subject and low-data methods solve a strictly harder problem.

**Why it breaks comparison.** A cross-subject method losing to a subject-specific one is not evidence that it is worse.

**How to check.** Record hours-of-target-subject-data as a column, not a footnote.

---
